9	from the documentation alone (constitution, Law 7). This file is the runtime-neutral entry
10	point: whatever agent family you are, arrival starts here.
11	
12	This document is conductor/session-tier. Cars do NOT read the corpus on arrival - a car is
13	**brief-bound**: it reads its brief and the contracts the brief names, nothing more. The
14	tiered reading path below is for the conductor and for a session being (re)established.
15	
16	## Tier 1 - mandatory (read in this order)
17	
18	1. [`docs/constitution.md`](docs/constitution.md) - the laws (Law 1-7) the whole shop obeys.
19	2. [`docs/the-healing-loop.md`](docs/the-healing-loop.md) - why the shop exists and how it heals.
20	3. [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) - the statute index (see "The statute index" heading): the
21	   working rules and the scars behind them. Runtime-neutral doctrine despite the filename.
22	4. [`docs/glossary.md`](docs/glossary.md) - the shared vocabulary (dispatch, subject, mint,
23	   adapter, fold, rung...). Read before the process docs so the terms land.
24	5. [`docs/setup.md`](docs/setup.md) - how to stand the harness up and which runtimes it runs under.
25	6. [`docs/doc-map.md`](docs/doc-map.md) - the map of every document and the reading paths through them.

28	
29	- The rung templates in [`docs/templates/`](docs/templates/) - the brief shapes for each rung

34	
35	- [`artifacts/reviews/`](artifacts/reviews/) - the landed verdicts: how prior work was judged.

38	## The compliance floor (non-negotiable, every agent, every rung)
39	
40	- **Envelope mandate + task-id echo.** End every report with the artifact envelope (a fenced
41	  block, info string `starcar-artifact`, carrying `outcome`, `findings`, `abstract`), and echo
42	  the minted dispatch id your brief delivered as `task-id`. That envelope is how your `returned`
43	  record obtains its outcome and pairs to its launch record. No angle brackets inside the block.
44	- **Carrier rule.** A finding is carried with its identifier so the next reviewer can trace it;
45	  reviewer work product is evidence, never discarded silently.
46	- **Never push (cars).** Cars commit LOCALLY on their branch and never push and never merge -
47	  the conductor merges.
48	- **Honest stop.** If your brief contradicts the real code, STOP on that item with file:line

51	- **TDD red-first.** For every behaviour change: write the failing test, RUN it, confirm it
52	  fails for the stated reason, then implement to green.
53	- **Verification honesty.** Claims are verifiable: exact pass counts, observed failures verbatim,
54	  commit SHAs, file:line citations. Never claim a thing verified that you have not watched pass.

batch 1 → [session-start-report] 2026-07-26T12:50:11Z / BATCH-1-GUARD-A / BATCH-1-GUARD-B

A Copilot agent reads a file whose timestamp line belongs to the *previous* session and whose content mixes two sessions, with nothing to tell them apart. Law 1 on the exact surface this feature exists to create.

Falsified claims, all still on disk: `.github/copilot-instructions.md:17` *"freshly truncated per session"*; `ONBOARDING.md:63` *"freshly truncated per session, first line a timestamp marker"*; and `.gitignore:2` *"freshly truncated per session"* — **added by commit `db1d3da` in this very fix cycle.** Round 1's `--reset` handled this case correctly, so this is a regression, and it is nowhere disclosed (I grepped the script, both design amendments, `docs/setup.md`, and both pointer files: no mention of `STALE_SECONDS`' consequence).

Not exotic: this repo's own doctrine enumerates *"a session resumes after compaction"* as a first-class trigger (`ONBOARDING.md:74`, `docs/setup.md:55`, design `:145`). Wall-clock proximity is not session identity, and no value of `STALE_SECONDS` makes it one.

### N2 — The `date -r` fallback the script calls "the safe default" loses 75% of guard output under concurrency.
`.claude/hooks/session-start-record.sh:96-98` (*"an unreadable/missing file or an unparseable result both fall through to 'stale' (reset), the safe default"*), `:102`.

`date -u -r FILE +%s` is GNU-specific. On BSD/macOS `date -r` takes a seconds argument; on busybox it is absent. **Injection E** (simulating that, reverted byte-identical): 4 concurrent guards × 10 trials —

```
RESULT: 30 / 40 guard outputs LOST
last trial's report: [session-start-report] 2026-07-26T12:51:14Z
                     GUARD-C-10
```

Falling through to *stale* on every invocation makes every guard truncate its predecessors; the mutex converts a race into deterministic total loss of all but the last. The "safe default" claim is false — and it is the fallback the whole M4 fix rests on. Round 1's mechanism had no `date` dependency at all. One-word remedy: on an undeterminable mtime, treat as **fresh** (a duplicate append is recoverable; a truncate is not), or use `find "$F" -mmin -1` / an `-nt` comparison instead of asking `date`.

### N3 — The mutex releases a lock it never acquired; the documented bound is 2.5x optimistic.
`.claude/hooks/session-start-record.sh:87-93` — the `trap 'rmdir "$LOCK_DIR"' EXIT` at `:93` is installed unconditionally, on the `break`-out (fail-open) path as well as on the acquire path.

Observed, slow guard vs fast guard:
```
t=1s     lock dir exists? YES   (slow guard holds it, still inside its critical section)
         fast guard wall time: 5126 ms   (header :84-85 documents "bounded (~2s)")
t=~3s    lock dir exists? NO - released by a process that never held it
```
So once any invocation fails open, the mutex is destroyed while the true holder is still running, and a third invocation can enter concurrently. `session-start-record.sh:40-44` asserts *"only one invocation's body runs at a time"* and `docs/setup.md:123-124` asserts the mutex means *"no guard's output can be lost"* — both stronger than the mechanism supports.

This is realistic, not theoretical: the lock is held across `tee`, i.e. for the **upstream guard's entire runtime**, and `session-start-ci-baseline.sh:24-39` makes a network `gh run list` call. Latency measured: leaked-lock batch **6563 ms** vs **515 ms** baseline — against a brief constraint of "trivial latency". *(I did not reproduce data loss through this path and do not claim it; the finding is that the guard's stated mutual-exclusion property is demonstrably false.)*

You're at the terminal per the notifier, so here's the escalation in full — **your ruling is the gate now; the reviewer capped further mechanism work and the doctrine binds me to honor it.**

## What happened

The fix cycle closed all eleven round-1 findings — the reviewer confirmed each one, several rated exemplary. But its round-2 pass found **four new Majors, every one created by the fixes**, three in the same file. Measured, not read: a second SessionStart within 60s appends the previous session's report instead of truncating; the `date -r` fallback silently loses 30/40 guard outputs on non-GNU systems; the mutex's EXIT trap releases a lock it never acquired. Two swirl triggers fired (same-file clustering, fix-created defects), so the reviewer set a cap: **no third mechanism revision**, and it escalated the premise that no round ever questioned.

## The premise, and your two questions

**The record script has been trying to determine "which session am I in" by itself — and it structurally cannot.** Its stdin is occupied by the guard output it's capturing, so it can never read the SessionStart payload that actually carries the session id. Round 1 proxied session identity with array ordering; round 2 with wall-clock mtime; both leaked. The reviewer's point: remove the premise and the problem dissolves.

**Q1 — what shape replaces it?** Four options, smallest-assumption first:

- **(d) Agent-pull, no mechanism at all (my recommendation):** revert settings.json to the bare four-guard wiring (the round-1 shape observed working under both runtimes), delete the record script entirely, and have the Copilot arrival doc say: *run the guard scripts as your first action and read the output*. One tiny runner script, no shared file, no truncation, no mutex, no session-identity question — N1/N2/N3 become structurally impossible. And it's honest about reliance: the current mechanism *already* depends on the Copilot agent following its arrival doc to read the report file; this depends on it exactly as much, minus all the machinery. Bonus: it's verifiable the moment any Copilot session runs the command — no longer restart-hook-gated.
- (c) Per-guard files a reader concatenates — no shared mutable file; still uses pipes whose Copilot behavior is unobserved.
- (a) Runtime-supplied batch key — needs a probe that may find nothing.
- (b) A dedicated truncation hook line — still ordering-dependent; weakest.

**Q2 — should Task 2 ship before the Copilot leg is ever observed?** Under (d) this mostly dissolves: there's nothing unobservable left to harden, and the first Copilot session verifies it live.

## Meanwhile

The cap-exempt fixes (N4 — the epoch floor silently vacated the divergence pin, plus two minors) are already running as a scoped round 3 with the mechanism explicitly frozen in the brief. The r2 verdict is landed, pushed green-watched (`af9da65`, 154 index rows), and the swirl catch is in the friction log — the cap fired *before* a third mechanism was written, which is precisely the scar the doctrine was built from.

One word on Q1 (a/b/c/d or your own shape) and I'll run the implementing round.

== #34: Chaos-monkey drills: unannounced disruption as standing practice (complement to the planned #21 series)
OWNER PRACTICE, named 2026-07-23: "I took that as a good chance to run another unannounced surprise drill. Chaos monkey the process."

#21 already covers the DRILL SERIES for conductor handoff: gentle, baseline, then adversarial - all PLANNED. This issue names the complementary practice the owner just exercised: unannounced, unplanned disruption, including converting an accident of the universe into a deliberate test.

WHAT HAPPENED (the first instance, and it was not planned by anyone)
The owner hit a monthly credit limit. Session `67913b32` died mid-work at 16:21:48 (git reflog on `car/31-register-css`), having cut a branch and worktree for issue #31 and written no checkpoint. The owner declined to smooth this over and instead let the next session ("pick up where we left off") run cold as a surprise drill.

WHAT IT CAUGHT - the value case for making this standing
1. The conductor invented a benign story for the debris ("a prior session prepared this and the checkpoint forgot to mention it") that fit the evidence and permitted work to continue, when the truth was a death. Logged, then corrected in the open.
2. The conductor improvised past a VISIBLE contradiction: RESUME-HERE said the #21 drill was "ARMED" for next session while commit 38b67c8's subject says it already PASSED. A checkpoint describing a future that had already happened is a stale document - a lying canary by this repo's own doctrine - and it was readable in the first two tool calls. `CLAUDE.md` lists improvising past a contradiction among the only REAL failures.
3. It surfaced #32 (the producer hook silently skipping 2 of 3 dispatches), which no instrument had reported and which is blind precisely in the killed-session case.

None of these were reachable by the planned drill, because the planned drill grades a GRACEFUL handoff - the easy case, and the one the process was designed for.

THE STRUCTURAL LESSON ALREADY APPLIED
A checkpoint written only at session end does not exist when the end is not graceful. Here's the decision package for the block — the live board actually hands us a perfect specimen for #30.

## #30 — conditions grouping + severity calibration (your taste needed)

**What the board shows right now:** two full-width `needs-attention` condition rows — `discovery: outcome: completed` and `discovery: outcome: approve-for-merge`. Those are the *sibling-family outcome words* — the vocabulary enum predates the cross-family work, so every Copilot-era outcome renders as a permanent alarm. Wolf-criers by construction, and the same class that once rendered 52 rows. My proposal, four parts:

1. **Group by class:** one row per condition class with a count — `discovery ×2`, expandable to details. Fifty-two identical drifts become one line.
2. **Severity per class, from the severity philosophy:** each condition class is declared NOTE-tier (expected patterns — vocabulary discoveries) or FLAG-tier (defects — integrity failures, unparseable records) in one owned mapping, pinned the way #37 pinned the register taxonomy. NOTEs render calm and collapsed; FLAGs render needs-attention.
3. **Placement:** the conditions strip becomes chrome — a single summary line ("1 FLAG + 2 notes") that expands, with the yard lanes staying above the fold. The glance reads the yard first.
4. **Quiet by declaration, never by ack-list:** a known discovery is silenced by *declaring* the new vocabulary value (the #26 pattern), so the condition disappears because it stopped being true — not because it was muted. First application: declare the sibling outcome words and today's two alarms vanish legitimately.

If that shape suits you, say go (and any placement preference) and I'll run the design → car → review cycle on it.

## #34 — chaos-monkey ratification (four open questions, my recommendations)

**Cadence:** opportunistic as the standing default (convert every real disruption into a graded drill — costs nothing), *plus* standing authorization for you to spring deliberate ones whenever — unannounced by definition, so there's no schedule to ratify, only the authority and the rubric. **Rubric:** the ticket's own — can the next session reconstruct from durable artifacts alone; what was lost is the score; a drill counts only if something LANDS. **Targets:** stay your whim — a published target list would un-chaos the monkey. If you ratify those three sentences, I land them as the doctrine section with the credit-limit kill as the founding scar.

## #21 — status check, then your call

Drill 1 (gentle) ran and **passed** on 07-23 — zero divergence, five claims re-derived cold. Drill 2 (baseline) is therefore already satisfied: the calibration record exists in the retro, and zero divergence meant no template fixes. What remains is **drill 3+, adversarial** — mid-train kills, pending-red handoffs — which is functionally the same practice #34 ratifies. ok #25 is a wiat for a bit. I have a question, how does the sibling project which runs on a very similar workflow adopt starcar?

#25 waits — noted on the board already. On the adoption question — it's a good one, and StarCar was quietly built for it. The answer has a short version and a real one.

**Short version:** the sibling doesn't install StarCar — it adopts the *contract* and copies the *tools*, then proves the fit by conformance rather than by trust. Everything portable lives in three directories that were deliberately built repo-relative and family-agnostic: `schema/` (the wire schema, the conformance vectors, the vocabularies — the contract), `scripts/` (producer, detector, verdict landing/verify, index, Watch-CI, the probe suites — the mechanism), and the hook wiring shapes (`.claude/settings.json` simple-form lines, the `.github/hooks` variant, `ONBOARDING.md` plus per-family pointer files — the front door). The board is optional at first; the store is useful alone, and their own board instance pointed at their own repo comes free when they want the glance.

**The real version, in the order I'd run it:**

1. **The vectors are the adoption instrument, not the scripts.** The store schema was deliberately left producer-open, and `schema/vectors/` exists precisely so an adopter doesn't have to trust our code — their harness either passes the conformance fixtures or the failures name exactly what their environment does differently. This is the "landed probes become the next layer's headers" doctrine working across repos: StarCar's landed schema is the header file the sibling checks first.
2. **The probe suites tell them what their substrate differs on.** Day one in the sibling repo, `scripts/probes/` reds by name for every substrate fact that doesn't hold on their boxes — that's the suite doing for them what it did for us, and today's ubuntu incident is the proof the class matters.
